name: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)
analogy: Think of it as finding the paint colours behind a set of paintings. Every painting is made by mixing a few base colours in different amounts, and you can only add paint, never remove it. The model discovers the base colours and how much of each every painting used.

steps.title: Arrange the data as a table of non-negative numbers
steps.description: The model needs a table where every value is zero or more, such as volumes, counts or ranges. Each row is an item, such as a trading day, and each column is a measurement, such as the volume in one time slot.
steps.inExample: The table has one row per trading day and six columns, each the total MNQ volume in one block of the day, for 250 days.

steps.title: Choose how many building blocks to find
steps.description: You pick a small number of building-block patterns. Fewer blocks give a simpler summary and more blocks reproduce the days more exactly.

steps.title: Start with random positive guesses
steps.description: The model begins with random positive guesses for the building blocks and for how much of each block each day uses. A smart start from a simpler decomposition is often used to get a stable answer.
steps.inExample: Three random positive volume shapes are drawn, and every day starts with equal amounts of each.

steps.title: Nudge the amounts to rebuild the days better
steps.description: Holding the blocks fixed, the amounts each day uses are adjusted so that mixing the blocks recreates the real days more closely. The updates multiply by a factor, which keeps every number positive.
steps.inExample: Days with a heavy opening get more of the opening-heavy block, and days with a busy close get more of the closing block.

steps.title: Nudge the blocks to rebuild the days better
steps.description: Then the blocks themselves are adjusted, holding the amounts fixed, to reduce the remaining difference between the rebuilt days and the real ones. Again every number stays positive.
steps.inExample: The opening-heavy block sharpens to put most of its volume in the first hour.

steps.title: Repeat until the rebuild stops improving
steps.description: The two nudging steps alternate until the gap between the rebuilt table and the real table stops shrinking. The result is a set of additive building blocks and a small table of amounts.
steps.inExample: After 300 rounds the average gap is about 6 percent of the volume.

steps.title: Read each block and score new items
steps.description: Because blocks can only add, each one is a readable pattern, such as a morning surge. A new day is described by how much of each block is needed to rebuild it, found by the same positive-only fitting.
steps.inExample: The new day needs 48 percent of the opening-heavy block, 17 percent of the midday-lull block and 35 percent of the closing-ramp block.

useFor.example: Breaking each day's volume profile into an opening surge, a midday lull and a closing ramp, and seeing how much of each a day contains.
Describing each trading day by three block amounts instead of six or 78 volume values, then feeding them to a model.

useFor.task: Spotting changes in how the day unfolds
useFor.example: Watching whether the share of the opening-surge block creeps up over months, a sign the daily rhythm is changing.
Splitting a matrix of trade counts by price level and time into a few recurring activity patterns.

avoidWhen: Your data can be negative, such as returns or standardized features; the method cannot handle negative values, so use principal component analysis or independent component analysis.
You want the best possible compression of variance; blocks are chosen for readability rather than ranking by importance, so principal component analysis compresses more tightly.

example.scenario: A researcher summarises how MNQ volume is spread across a regular trading day, using 250 days and three building blocks, and then decomposes one new day.

input.summary: Total volume in six blocks of the day for the new day, in contracts.

fields.name: volume in block 1, first hour
fields.meaning: Contracts traded during the first hour of the day, usually the busiest.

fields.name: volume in block 2
fields.meaning: Contracts traded in the second hour.

fields.name: volume in block 3
fields.meaning: Contracts traded in the third hour, near the midday lull.

fields.name: volume in block 4
fields.meaning: Contracts traded in the fourth hour, the quietest stretch.

fields.name: volume in block 5
fields.meaning: Contracts traded in the fifth hour as activity returns.

fields.name: volume in block 6, final stretch
fields.meaning: Contracts traded in the closing stretch, also usually busy.

fields.name: building blocks requested
fields.meaning: How many patterns the model was asked to find.

output.summary: How much of each building-block pattern the day needs, and how well the rebuild matches.

fields.name: share from the opening-surge pattern
fields.meaning: How much of the day's volume is explained by the pattern concentrated in the first hour.

fields.name: share from the midday-lull pattern
fields.meaning: How much is explained by the flat, low-volume pattern through the middle of the day.

fields.name: share from the closing-ramp pattern
fields.meaning: How much is explained by the pattern rising into the close.

fields.name: rebuild gap
fields.meaning: How far the volume rebuilt from the three patterns differs from the actual day.

example.reading: This was an opening-heavy day with a busy close and a short lull: close to half its volume follows the opening-surge pattern. Use the three shares as day-type features, and watch the rebuild gap, because a large gap means the day has a shape the three patterns do not capture.
